catalog_citation: Tabain, Marija & Gertrud Schneider-Blum. 2024 [online 14 Nov 2023]. Tima (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 54: 515-539. doi:10.1017/S0025100323000257 (CC BY 4.0). Saved file: the copy we hold
catalog_locator: section 'Tones', printed p. 532 (PDF p. 18), continuing pp. 533-534; 'Syllable structure' p. 534 (PDF p. 20); identity p. 515 (PDF p. 1)
catalog_quote: Though a thorough tonal analysis of Tima is still pending, we can say with some confidence that Tima has a two-tone system, H and L (High and Low), with an additional downstepped high tone ↓H (the conditions for which are described below). The tone-bearing unit is usually a vowel but may be a syllabic nasal at the beginning of the word or a sonorant coda. In addition, the H and L tones can combine on the syllable rhyme (i.e. on a long vowel nucleus; or on a short vowel nucleus plus sonorant coda) to produce rising LH and falling HL tones. ... Tone can be used to produce minimal pairs at the lexical level (e.g. within the noun class) or at the grammatical level (e.g. noun versus verb; single action versus pluractionality; telic/atelic distinction). Minimal or near-minimal pairs in tone are quite common in Tima. ... In summary, the tonal system is characterized by a rather complex system …
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (25 pp., text layer, JIPA 54: 515-539, CC BY). PDF p. 18 = printed p. 532, section heading 'Tones'. The quoted passage is there verbatim: 'Though a thorough tonal analysis of Tima is still pending, we can say with some confidence that Tima has a two-tone system, H and L (High and Low), with an additional downstepped high tone ↓H (the conditions for which are described below). The tone-bearing unit is usually a vowel but may be a syllabic nasal at the beginning of the word or a sonorant coda.' then, after the reader's [..] (which skips two sentences on LH/HL contours on bimoraic rhymes and the exceptional word /kàɡááɡâk/), 'Tone can be used to produce minimal pairs at the lexical leve…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tima is a lexical- and grammatical-tone language (H, L, downstepped H; LH and HL contours on bimoraic rhymes). The IPA Illustration, the only full published phonological sketch that is open, has no stress or accent section and never uses the word 'stress'; no source opened states where word stress falls or whether stress exists. The only positional tendencies reported are tonal: contour tones favour the last syllable of polysyllabic words, and polysyllabic (mostly nominal) words tend to begin Low (p. 534).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: one word /kàɡááɡâk/ with a falling tone on a short vowel before /k/ is flagged as unexplained; downstepped H is treated as non-tonemic except in a few lexicalized items (p. 532-533).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical and grammatical tone; downstep also across syntactic boundaries. Schneider-Blum 2022 (LLA 8(2), fn. 4) adds that 'Tone in Tima has not yet been systematically investigated' and that examples are marked phonetically on citation forms (verbs cited in the imperative singular). Illustration data: 3 male speakers, f0 measured at vowel midpoints (2326 tokens).
new_statements.identity_note: Tima proper (tima1241, ISO tms), the sole member of Katla-Tima named Tima; JIPA data from Tima speakers of the Tima hills (three male speakers for the acoustic tone data). No dialect issue; the related Katla (katl1237) is a different language and not described here.
